questions.q: Why does columnar storage (Parquet) suit quant analytical queries better than row-oriented storage (CSV)?
options: Columnar files can only store numeric data, which is all quant workflows need
Quant queries typically read a few columns across many rows; columnar storage lets you read one contiguous block per needed column and skip the rest
CSV files cannot be opened by pandas at all
Columnar storage eliminates the need for any compression
questions.explain: Parquet stores each column's values contiguously, so reading just 'price' and 'volume' out of a wide table means reading only those blocks, skipping everything else on disk — exactly the access pattern most analytical queries need.

questions.q: What role does `pyarrow` play between pandas, Polars, and a Parquet file on disk?
options: It is an unrelated plotting library with no connection to Parquet
It implements the Arrow in-memory format and the Parquet reader/writer that both pandas and Polars rely on, which is why conversions between them are often cheap
It converts Parquet files into CSV before pandas can read them
It is required only for writing Parquet, never for reading it
questions.explain: pyarrow implements Arrow (the shared in-memory columnar format) and Parquet I/O. Because pandas (via pyarrow) and Polars both use Arrow, moving data between them or to/from a Parquet file often requires no reshaping, just reinterpretation.

It skips reading the data blocks for every other column entirely, rather than reading everything and dropping columns afterward
It sorts the DataFrame by date and price
It has no effect unless filters is also specified
questions.explain: This is column pruning: the Parquet reader only reads the requested columns' data blocks from disk, avoiding the cost of reading and then discarding unneeded columns.

questions.q: What is predicate pushdown, as applied via the `filters` argument to `read_parquet`?
options: Filtering the resulting DataFrame in pandas after the entire file has already been loaded
Pushing the row-level filter into the Parquet reader itself, which uses per-row-group statistics to skip chunks that can't possibly match
A way to rename columns during the read
A technique that only works with the zstd compression codec
questions.explain: Predicate pushdown applies the filter during the read, letting the reader use file-level statistics to skip entire row groups that cannot contain matching rows — avoiding the work rather than doing it after the fact.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off between the snappy and zstd compression codecs for Parquet?
options: snappy is faster to compress/decompress with a modest ratio; zstd compresses more slowly but achieves noticeably smaller files
zstd is always faster and smaller in every case, with no downside
snappy only works with integer columns; zstd only works with strings
They produce identical file sizes; the choice is purely about compatibility
questions.explain: snappy favors speed with a modest compression ratio, making it a solid default for frequently-read files, while zstd trades slower write-time compression for a noticeably smaller file, useful when storage or transfer cost matters more.
